canonical_statement: The study investigates why agentic coding context files accumulate instructions and whether prompt comments that preserve latent rationale can prevent this growth.

The paper models prompt maintenance as online estimation of an unobservable constraint set from censored, noisy feedback, with prompt quality evaluated on correctness and excess size relative to a minimum cover.

The model states that auditing whether an instruction is excess can require testing subsets of the prompt, giving an O(2^|D|) counterfactual search in the general case, whereas preserved latent reasoning reduces the relevant check to O(1).
The authors name the divergence caused by decaying recoverability of instruction rationale catastrophic remembering and derive that equilibrium prompt size diverges as recoverability approaches zero.
The observational corpus spans 1,867 public GitHub repositories carrying CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, or copilot-instructions.md files.

population.label: Public GitHub repositories with agentic context files

canonical_statement: The corpus contains 1,801 multi-version context files, 299,440 version-to-version transitions, and 247,694 tracked instruction lifetimes.
Instructions are segmented at clause-level imperative boundaries and matched across versions by exact, normalized, then fuzzy matching; the fuzzy similarity threshold is 70.
On 50 hand-annotated transitions, the cross-version instruction matcher achieved 1.000 precision and 0.933 recall.

A rewrite is defined as a commit in which at least 50% of a file’s live instructions die, subject to a floor of five instructions at risk; text reappearing in a sibling file at the same commit is treated as migration, and both are censored as competing risks for deletion-hazard estimation.
The rewrite and migration competing-risk rules censor 77.3% of observed instruction deaths.

concept.text: Share of deaths censored as competing risks

canonical_statement: At the last tracked version, the median context file contains 39 instructions and the 90th percentile contains 131 instructions.

concept.text: Instruction count at last tracked version

canonical_statement: Among 1,576 multi-version repositories, 64.3% increased instruction count and 26.6% decreased it, with a median net gain of seven instructions.
Excluding mass rewrites, 19,267 commits add an average net 4.9 instructions per commit.
Over normalized file lifetime, mean instruction count rises by 226%, mean instruction length by 10%, and total agentic-prompt size by 140%.
Rewrite and sibling-file migration events account for 77.3% of instruction deaths, including 96,162 rewrite deaths and 682 migration deaths.
After censoring rewrites and migrations, 247,694 instruction lifetimes remain with 28,426 tracked deletions for deletion-hazard analysis.

population.label: Instruction lifetimes retained for hazard analysis

canonical_statement: At the first mass rewrite, mean instruction count falls to 59.5% of its pre-rewrite level and recovers to 91.5% within 10 subsequent commits.

concept.text: Instruction count relative to pre-rewrite level

canonical_statement: Files grow at 4.1% per commit before their first rewrite and 4.9% per commit after it.
Deletion hazard declines with instruction age with a log-hazard slope of -0.032 per commit and a 95% interval from -0.047 to -0.019.

In the gamma-frailty analysis of recurring instruction text, content-shared frailty absorbs 30.8% of the no-frailty age slope while the residual slope remains -0.0355 with a 95% interval from -0.0414 to -0.0296.

concept.text: Instruction age with shared-text gamma frailty

canonical_statement: In an exploratory piecewise-exponential hazard model, the multi-author-by-age interaction is -0.0211 with z=-11.7 and a 95% interval from -0.0246 to -0.0175.

concept.text: Multi-author file status interacted with instruction age

outcome.measurement_method: Piecewise-exponential hazard with file gamma frailty

canonical_statement: The corpus pre-registration gates all pass, including median per-repository net change +7, grow-to-shrink ratio 2.42, 28,426 deletions excluding rewrites, and 57.0% of deletions at or above median instruction age.
Across 1,353 rewrite commits, the median event kills 46 instructions and births 14; 24.4% leave the file empty, 38.3% replace at least half the dead text, and 2.9% carry any cross-file migration.

arms.arm_label: replace at least half dead text

canonical_statement: Inverse-IFEval hides each benchmark item’s stated instructions as the known reference minimum cover, retains the verifiers as hidden constraints, and supplies the maintainer only a generated general objective plus censored feedback.
The canonical Inverse-IFEval testbed uses 184 eligible worlds per seed and three seeds, yielding 552 maintenance histories per arm; covers contain two instructions in 423 histories and three in 129.

Each Inverse-IFEval history runs for 15 maintenance steps; at every step a fresh maintainer receives the persisted prompt and arm-specific handoff, while the executor sees the prompt with comments removed.
The canonical controlled experiment uses claude-haiku-4-5 as both maintainer and executor and offers no instruction-rewording operation, so each instruction has an unambiguous age.
The comment channel is attached only to live instructions, has a 1,024-character budget, is visible to subsequent maintainers, and is stripped by code before executor inference.
The harness rejects instruction text that cites past failures, verification results, or maintenance steps, preventing arms from routing provenance through the executable instruction body.
At 15 maintenance steps across 552 histories, informative comments end at -5.8% excess size versus +60.4% without comments, with last-three-round constraint satisfaction 38.2% versus 39.0%.

concept.text: Final excess size at approximately parity constraint satisfaction

canonical_statement: At 51 maintenance steps across 184 histories, informative comments end at +1.4% excess size versus +211.3% without comments, while both arms have 44.0% constraint satisfaction.

concept.text: Final excess size at parity constraint satisfaction

canonical_statement: Using the Table 2 values, the absolute excess-size difference between no comments and informative comments at 51 steps is 209.9 percentage points.

concept.text: Absolute difference in final excess size

canonical_statement: The paper reports that informative comments remove 99.3% of excess instructions at 51 steps, comparing +211.3% excess without comments with +1.4% with informative comments.
By cover-size stratum at 15 steps, no-comment excess is +74.2% for two-instruction covers and +15.2% for three-instruction covers, while informative-comment excess is -1.1% and -21.2%, respectively.

canonical_statement: Across three maintainer capability tiers, uncommented final size ratios rise from 1.68 with Haiku 4.5 to 3.07 with Sonnet 5 and 6.72 with Opus 5; the comment protocol reduces excess size relative to each control by 42.1%, 61.7%, and 52.3%, respectively.

canonical_statement: In comment-content ablations, comment-shaped noise changes excess size by -3.1% versus control, narrative without outcomes by +8.8%, and the full COMMIT schema by -48.9%.

canonical_statement: Dropping the recurrence-count field from the full comment schema reduces its excess-size effect from -48.9% to -30.9%.

The three canonical Inverse-IFEval world draws reproduce the ratchet criterion separately; no-comment excess is +59.9%, +49.8%, and +71.6%, with pooled +60.4% and across-seed standard deviation 10.9 percentage points.

concept.text: Final excess size across independent world draws

canonical_statement: At the per-world level, informative comments have mean final size ratio 0.942 and mean absolute distance from cover 0.481, but end with an empty prompt in 12.1% of worlds.

Among the 67 worlds where the informative-comment protocol empties the prompt, its satisfaction is 0.259 versus 0.279 for no comments and 0.328 for comment-shaped noise; the paired noise-minus-protocol difference is -0.070 from the protocol perspective with 95% interval -0.114 to -0.027.

When comments are exposed to the executor instead of stripped, final excess is +28.5% versus -0.1% in the canonical stripped run, an excess-size difference of 28.6 percentage points with a 95% interval from 5.5 to 58.5, without a resolved satisfaction benefit.

The WildIFEval experiment seeds each world with all but K true instructions plus G distractor instructions drawn from other items, then scores human-written constraints with an arm-blind LLM judge that sees one constraint and one response but no prompt, arm label, history, or sibling constraints.
Across 64 WildIFEval worlds with K=1 and G=16, seeded distractors reduce true-instruction satisfaction from 65.6% at G=0 to 41.5%, a 24.1-percentage-point loss with 95% interval -33.4 to -14.9.
Over three WildIFEval maintenance rounds, informative comments increase constraint satisfaction from 50.4% to 62.0%, an 11.6-percentage-point improvement with a 95% interval from 5.1 to 18.3.
The 11.6-percentage-point WildIFEval gain corresponds to a reported 23.1% relative improvement in instruction-following.
Comment-shaped noise differs from the uncommented WildIFEval arm by 2.7 percentage points, with a 95% interval from -4.4 to 10.1 that includes zero.

Re-scoring all 6,336 WildIFEval verdicts with a second judge yields a comments-versus-control effect of 7.8 percentage points versus 11.6 with the first judge; the difference-in-differences is 3.8 percentage points with a 95% interval from -1.9 to 9.6.
The two WildIFEval judges agree on 82.1% of 6,336 verdicts, with Cohen kappa 0.639 and a 95% interval from 0.620 to 0.657; marginal pass rates are 0.545 and 0.547.

The controlled experiment uses 49,680 model calls, 37.9 million tokens, and 45 model-hours across both roles, three seeds, and three arms; the authors report no model training and CPU-only cloud containers for the non-hosted portions.

The authors state that they redistribute no repository content and release derived per-instruction tables plus code that rebuilds them from public repository histories; exact dependency versions are frozen in a lockfile.

The observational analysis fixes the 50% rewrite threshold, validates the matcher on only 50 hand-annotated transitions out of 299,440 tracked transitions, and uses a corpus-specific segmentation grammar that was not independently varied.

The controlled Inverse-IFEval experiment uses covers of only two or three instructions, a 15-step canonical horizon, one model as both maintainer and executor, and mechanically verifiable English constraints, whereas the median field context file has 39 instructions.

The WildIFEval experiment seeds excess instructions into benchmark prompts rather than observing the ratchet grow naturally at that scale, so it estimates the cost of excess and the recovery from comments rather than persistence of real-file growth.

WildIFEval satisfaction is scored by LLM judges; a second judge reproduces the direction and yields substantial agreement, but neither judge is ground truth and no human-annotated accuracy subsample was run.

The corpus is limited to public GitHub agent context files; the study does not measure natural-language or programming-language distributions, does not establish results for non-English instructions, and does not test system prompts or agent skill files.

The multi-author interaction is exploratory, was not pre-registered, uses one specification, and proxies turnover by counting distinct human editors rather than observing whether an instruction’s original author has left.

The authors conclude that agentic prompts grow because instruction rationale decays faster than the instruction itself and that preserving this rationale in prompt comments can reduce prompt size and recover instruction-following.
The authors characterize their prompt-comment implementation as a prototype and call for testing at representative constraint counts and with constraints that are not mechanically verifiable.

The authors warn that automated deletion based on recovered rationale can remove valid instructions; they recommend keeping a human in the deletion path and excluding safety-relevant instructions until the protocol is tested on them.

The paper states that LLMs were used for technical execution, writing, research support, and co-generation of code and appendix text, but a programmatic generator emitted every reported number and no LLM produced a reported value.
The authors reduce commit authorship metadata to a distinct-editor count during extraction and state that released artifacts carry no names or email addresses.
